title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
content: Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday. While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move. "The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained." With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history. Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading. The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google. That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn. SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year. Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks. Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned. The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together. Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more. Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger. He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX. Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield". He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve". Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion. While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics. SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.

title: Jobless rate falls but small firms cut back hiring
content: The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year. However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring. The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring. ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment". "The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said. "The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor." Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff. The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs. Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms. Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty". However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment". The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added. But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X that "businesses can't afford to hire". "This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said. The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year. Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment. Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover". But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said. Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened". But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising". The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body . The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates. In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics.

It also highlights the impact of rising labour costs on smaller businesses' hiring decisions, which is a relevant and timely issue for the category.
